articles.title: Tamil Nadu to set up Olympic City, Motor Sports City: All you need to know
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Tamil Nadu is set to establish an Olympic City and a Motor Sports City as part of its plans to create modern sports infrastructure and promot.
articles.body: CHENNAI: Tamil Nadu is set to establish an Olympic City and a Motor Sports City as part of its plans to create modern sports infrastructure and promote sports-related activities in the state.The Tamil Nadu Olympic City will have international-standard sports arenas, a High Performance Training Centre and accommodation facilities for sportspersons and coaches.It aims to provide better training and competition facilities and develop athletes capable of competing at national and international levels.A separate Motor Sports City will have a state-of-the-art motorsports complex and supporting infrastructure. Facilities will be created to host Formula 1, Formula 2, Formula 3 and Formula 4 races.It will also provide training opportunities and help identify and develop young motorsport talent.The Motor Sports City is expected to attract leading motor racing and car manufacturing companies to the state. articles.title: Ashes ticket price increase 'really poor' - Vaughan
articles.summary: Former England captain Michael Vaughan is critical of a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston.
articles.body:
Former England captain Michael Vaughan has called a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston "really poor".

The Birmingham ground will host the third Test of the best-of-five series between England and Australia next summer with ticket prices in the Hollies Stand - which holds almost 6,000 spectators - costing £165, up from £115 in 2023.

Elsewhere in the stadium, members can purchase tickets for £92, but the cheapest adult tickets across the first three days are £115, with every ticket carrying a £2.50 booking fee.

"This is really poor," Vaughan posted on social media in response to the news.

Following the 2023 series, which ended in a 2-2 draw after Australia won the first two Tests (at Edgbaston and Lord's), the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) said "every day sold out in advance, with total attendance topping 545,000".

Despite Warwickshire's Edgbaston stadium being at a reduced capacity because of the construction of an on-site hotel, tickets for next week's third Test between England and Pakistan, which range between £57.50-£87.50 for adults, have not sold out.

The ticket ballot for the 2027 Ashes opened on Wednesday, with prices more expensive at Lord's and the Oval in London, with the best tickets at £190 and £185.

England, who lost 4-1 in Australia last winter, begin their quest to regain the Ashes at Trent Bridge in Nottingham on 18 June.

The second Ashes Test at Lord's begins on 30 June and the third at Edgbaston on 8 July.

The Utilita Bowl in Southampton will become the 10th UK ground to host a men's Ashes Test when the fourth Test gets under way on 21 July, with the series concluding at the Kia Oval from 29 July.

BBC Sport has contacted the ECB and the five Test venues for comment.

Ticket prices for sporting events have been an ongoing point of contention for fans.

A crowd of 13,623 were at Birmingham's 23,000-capacity Alexander Stadium to watch Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt win the women's 100m at the European Athletics Championships last month.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with Category A tickets for the home straight costing £150.

For the men's 100m final those same seats cost £110, again with no concessions for juniors.

In April, Ryder Cup organisers defended ticket prices for next year's centenary golf event between Europe and the United States in Ireland.

Daily general admission tickets for the three tournament days on 17-19 September at Adare Manor in County Limerick will cost 499 euros (£434), compared with up to 260 euros in Italy in 2023.

articles.title: Neeraj Chopra replaced by CWG bronze medallist Yashvir Singh as AFI announces 77-member squad for Asian Games
articles.summary: More sports News: Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has replaced injured Neeraj Chopra in India's athletics squad for the upcoming Asian.
articles.body: Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has replaced injured Neeraj Chopra in India's athletics squad for the upcoming Asian Games in Japan, while long-distance runner Abhishek Pal has been dropped after receiving a notice from the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) over an alleged doping offence.The Athletics Federation of India (AFI) on Thursday announced a 77-member Indian track and field team for the September 19-October 4 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The announcement was made during a press conference in Ludhiana, which is hosting the National Youth Championships.Men's 110m hurdler Tejas Shirse has also been left out of the squad after suffering an injury during the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.AFI president Bahadur Singh Sagoo said Yashvir was brought in because Neeraj is unavailable due to injury."We have brought in Yashvir who is a CWG medal winner in place of Neeraj Chopra who is currently injured. It was an injury replacement and so there was no problem (in Yashvir coming in)," Sagoo said.He also confirmed that Abhishek Pal has been removed from the squad."Long distance runner Abhishek Pal has been dropped because of the issues he is facing. So this is the final team for the Asian Games," he added.Last month, Abhishek received a notice from NADA after his sample was found to contain a female fertility drug. Officials said the substance was present below the threshold level.Former AFI secretary and planning commission chief Lalit Bhanot said the federation did not want to take any risk while the investigation is ongoing."It's not a case of (Abhishek) returning dope positive. The presence of the substance is below threshold level. NADA is currently undergoing investigation. But we did not want to take any risk. We don't want anybody to point a finger on us. So, we have dropped Abhishek from the team," Bhanot said, as quoted by news agency PTI.Shirse and Abhishek were part of the 73-member squad announced by the sports ministry earlier this month. On Wednesday, the ministry added six more athletes to the athletics contingent.The six athletes added are Harita Bhadra (200m), Kiran Pahal (400m), Sindhushree G (pole vault), I Asha Ilango (triple jump), Sanya Yadav (discus throw) and Praveen Kumar (hammer throw).With two athletes dropped and six added, India's final athletics squad now has 77 members.The AFI has also requested permission for Avinash Sable to compete in the men's 5,000m in addition to his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event.Sable, who won gold in the steeplechase and silver in the 5,000m at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, has raced only once this season after recovering from ACL surgery."Sable's participation in 3000m steeplechase is confirmed, there is no problem in that. But we have also made a request to the Asian Games organisers for him to run in 5000m also."But, this is subject to him breaching the AFI qualification mark (in 5000m) during the final event of the Indian Athletics Series on September 10 in New Delhi," Bhanot said.The Indian Athletics Series Finals in New Delhi on September 10 will be a prize-money event, with most Asian Games-bound athletes expected to compete.The final squad also includes Gulveer Singh and Parul Chaudhary in three events each. Gulveer will compete in the 10,000m, 5,000m and 1,500m, while Parul will run the 3,000m steeplechase, 5,000m and 1,500m.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: American Olympics winner Tara Davis-Woodhall reveals she is ‘lucky to be alive’ after devastating crash
articles.summary: International Sports News: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall has revealed that she is “lucky and blessed to be alive” after being involved in a serious car crash. T.
articles.body: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall has revealed that she is “lucky and blessed to be alive” after being involved in a serious car crash. The American track and field star suffered a severe concussion after a head-on collision while driving to training last week. Both vehicles were badly damaged in the accident.The 27-year-old won long jump gold at the Paris Olympics 2024 and is now facing an uncertain period ahead of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship. Davis-Woodhall has not trained since the crash and said she is taking her recovery “day by day” after consulting doctors and physiotherapists.Tara Davis-Woodhall details scary car crash and training setbackTara Davis-Woodhall explained that the accident happened when she pulled into a parking lot while travelling at around 20mph. Another woman reportedly made a turn, resulting in the two vehicles crashing into each other.The impact was serious enough to write off both cars. Davis-Woodhall suffered a severe concussion but said she did not sustain any life-threatening injuries.“I pulled into the parking lot, and this lady just made a turn. We were both going about 20mph, so both of our cars were totalled. It’s very scary. I’m lucky and blessed to be alive and with no life-threatening injuries”, she said per The Sun.The accident has come at a difficult time for the Olympic champion. Davis-Woodhall was preparing for the World Athletics Ultimate Championship and believes she was in excellent form before the crash.The inaugural event is expected to bring together some of the biggest names in athletics. Winners of each event are set to receive a £111,000 prize ($150K).However, Davis-Woodhall’s participation is now uncertain. She has not returned to training since the accident.She has been working with doctors and physiotherapists to determine when she can safely resume her preparation.“I haven’t trained at all due to [the crash]. I’ve seen my doctors and my physios, and everyone’s just trying to get me back into it”, she added.Davis-Woodhall said she is physically recovering, but the accident has also affected her mentally.The timing has been especially frustrating for the American athlete. She said she was performing at the highest level of her career before the accident.“It’s really unfortunate timing. I’m at the peak of my training right now. I’m as fast as I’ve ever been. I’m as strong as I’ve ever been”, she discussed.Davis-Woodhall’s career-best long jump is 7.20 metres. She became one of the biggest stars in American athletics after winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024.She is also known for her relationship with Paralympic champion Hunter Woodhall, whom she married. The couple have become prominent figures in track and field and have a large following.Davis-Woodhall most recently competed at the USATF Outdoor Championships in July. She finished third in both the long jump and the 100m hurdles.Her immediate focus is now recovery rather than competition. With the World Athletics Ultimate Championship approaching, she does not yet know whether she will be able to compete.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: La española Pepi Sánchez Quintana, oro mundial de 400 metros... ¡a los 76 años!
articles.standfirst: Se impuso en la final del campeonato Master, que se disputa estos días en Daegu, con un tiempo de 1:25.33
articles.summary: Se impuso en la final del campeonato Master, que se disputa estos días en Daegu, con un tiempo de 1:25.33
articles.body: Pepi Sánchez Quintana sigue aumentando los éxitos en su palmarés. El último ha sido el oro que ha ganado en los 400 metros del Campeonato del Mundo de Master, que se disputa estos días en Daegu, a sus 76 años. La atleta andaluza se impuso en la final de la categoría, de F75, con un tiempo de 1:25.33, tras adelantar al esprint a la británica Roberts en los metros finales a la recta. Quintana, que llegó al atletismo hace unos años desde la bicicleta, continúa cosechando éxitos en la categoría Master. Ya en 2021 conquistó los títulos de España de 400 y 800 metros de su categoría, con sendos récords nacionales de ambas distancias en la categoría M70, con marcas de 1:27 y 3:22, respectivamente.

articles.title: New Formula 1 Track Proposed as India Expands Motorsport Ambitions
articles.summary: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has proposed a ‘Motor Sports City’ in his state along with Olympic City, to bolster the motor racing infrastructure,...
articles.body:
Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has proposed a 'Motor Sports City' in his state along with Olympic City, to bolster the motor racing infrastructure, with an F1 track in mind.

While India's only F1 track Buddh International Circuit is looking for a revival in the coming years via new investment from Adani Group, Tamil Nadu CM Vijay has proposed a 'Motor Sports City' in his state to add and enhance the existing onto the motorsport culture.

He proposed the same during his speech in the Assembly on Thursday under Rule 110. Apart from other proposals, the Motor Sports City got an approval from India's first-ever F1 driver Narain Karthikeyan after he re-shared the speech on his Instagram handle.

No more details has been laid out by Vijay, but only a proposal to create a world-class facility that will not just house F1, but also the feeder competitions like Formula 2, Formula 3 and Formula 4. Basically, he wants to create a hub of racing in Tamil Nadu.

This will include race tracks and world class training facilities, to tap and develop young talent to compete at national and international levels in the time to come. Tamil Nadu already houses FIA Grade 2 & Grade 4 circuits in Chennai and Coimbatore, repsectively.

Both the Madras Motor Race Track in Chennai and Kari Motor Speedway in Coimbatore runs Indian national events and has hosted international events like F4 South East Asia and Asia Road Racing Championship (two-wheeler racing).

Vijay highlighted Tamil Nadu's leading capacity in production of four-wheel and two-wheel cars. In fact, the MMRT circuit is opposite to a huge Hyundai facility. Even for motor racing, he noted about key manufacturing units are based near KMS circuit.

He wants to tap on the potential and provide greater facilities for youngsters, whether as racers and or mechanics/engineers, to practice their skills and represent India at the larger stage. It is to be seen if the city will be an extension to Olympic City.

While the proposal is in place, it will be too early to jump on the F1 bandwagon just yet. Even the return of Indian GP to BIC seems like 2-3 years away while Adani Group battles out for ownership. There are positive indications, but still in discussions stage.

articles.title: Letsile Tebogo: Ultimate Championships provide emotional return to Budapest
articles.summary: Letsile Tebogo says his late mother is always with him "in spirit" as he prepares to run in Budapest, the city where she watched him make history for Botswana and Africa.
articles.body:
Olympic 200m champion Letsile Tebogo will return to Budapest for the Ultimate Championships next week, but the Hungarian capital is more than just another stop on the athletics calendar for the Botswana sprinter.

It is the city where the 23-year-old announced himself to the world and where his mother Seratiwa watched him make history for his country by claiming two medals at the 2023 World Championships.

This time Seratiwa will not be cheering on her son from the stands, having passed away in May 2024 after a short illness.

Having shared a close relationship with his mother - one she described as being more like a "brother and sister bond" - Tebogo admits that returning without her is difficult.

"I haven't really looked into the fact that I'm going now to Budapest without my mom," he said.

"It's just been a bumpy ride having to think about it and having to continue with the grind."

Three years ago, Seratiwa surprised her son by travelling to Budapest to watch the then 20-year-old compete in his first senior global championships.

Tebogo won silver in the 100m and bronze in the 200m - the first World Championship medals claimed by a male athlete from Botswana. He also became the first African man to win a World Championship medal in the 100m.

Seratiwa told BBC Sport Africa at the time that she was "proud" of what her son had achieved.

For all the memories the city holds, Tebogo says there is also a source of strength in returning to the place where his mother witnessed one of the defining moments of his career.

"I believe she's always there with me in spirit and in days where giving up is an option," he said.

"She pushes me to give my absolute best and I believe the memories that we had in Budapest, they will still come again."

African athletes need support and protection - Kebinatshipi

Botswana welcomes Tebogo home with stadium spectacular

Those memories now sit alongside everything that has happened since for Tebogo.

A year on from his success at the 2023 World Championships, Tebogo scaled greater heights by becoming Botswana's first Olympic champion when he won the 200m at the Paris 2024 Games, carrying his mother's initials on both his shoes and fingernails as a tribute.

He returns to Budapest as one of the faces of a new competition created to bring together the sport's best performers.

The Ultimate Championships is a biennial global event designed to crown the best of the best in a track and field season.

The three-day end-of-season competition includes Olympic champions, world champions, Diamond League winners and the year's other leading performers.

The inaugural edition in Budapest, which runs from 11-13 September, has a $10m (£7.41m) prize pot - the highest in track and field history according to organisers World Athletics - with each gold medallist taking home $150,000 (£111,000).

Tebogo, who helped Botswana to gold in the 4x400m at the World Relays on home soil earlier this year before registering 200m wins at the Diamond League events in Oslo and Lausanne, says the 200m in Budapest will not only be about looking back.

He is one of the team captains for the Kids' Athletics Ultimate Challenge, where young people from across the city will be invited to participate in activities at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre the day before the Ultimate Championships begin.

That will give him the chance to share some of the lessons he has learned since first stepping onto the global stage.

"I believe firstly you should start with accountability," he said.

"Think about your preparation, how you want your journey or your season to be, and then also think of unwavering sportsmanship.

"I would love them to have that unwavering sportsmanship, so that they can share lanes, they can cheer for one another."

articles.title: From a below-average shooter to Olympic gold-winning coach: How Jelena Arunovic brought a new energy to India’s shooting camp
articles.summary: More sports News: In a parallel world, Jelena Arunovic could be a time traveller. One moment, the pistol coach could be seen reading a newspaper, scanning it thoroughly.
articles.body: In a parallel world, Jelena Arunovic could be a time traveller. One moment, the pistol coach could be seen reading a newspaper, scanning it thoroughly, making her shooters do it too. In the next, she could be sneakily taking photos to upload on her ‘insta’ stories.While reading newspapers probably make her one of the most aware persons in the Indian shooting setup, her selfies allow her to bond with the shooters, who train with her for hours, every day at the national camp in Bhopal.The shooter-turned-coach is bringing in a new energy, and it is contagious. She is breaking norms by becoming a cheerleader, friend to the shooters, while also maintaining her stature as pistol shooting coach.The Serbian has come to India after successfully coaching her sister Zorana and Damir Mikec to 10m air pistol mixed team gold at the Paris Games. After her stint with the Serbian national team, Jelena worked as the head coach of Guangdong Province in China.“I have some experience with Asian teams — last year, I was in China — but this is completely different. Everything is more intense, not just with the national team but in general, from food to everything else. So far, I like it,” Jelena, 45, told TOI.The Serbian is getting used to India’s way of over-reaction. “Everything is very emotional. The intensity is five times bigger when we are sad, when we are happy, when we celebrate. Everything is over the top. When we are happy, we are very happy. When we are sad, it’s the end of the world. I’m still adapting,” she confessed.“I’m still trying to find similarities with the Serbian national team and with Chinese athletes and trying to change myself also so I can fit in better and give better results,” she said.Jelena participated in world competitions from 1997 to 2012, she took up coaching after retiring from active shooting. On how the two experiences were different, the Serb said both her roles are incomparable. “These experiences are completely different. As an athlete, I was below average. I have only one medal, a silver from the World Championships in Olympic disciplines. I never mention that because I think it’s rude to mention my personal experience when you have such a good group of athletes. How can they relate to one medal from the World Championships?” she admitted.“But as a coach, my experience is on a completely different level. I have won everything. That is the thing that I'm the proudest of, because I know how difficult it was for me and my sister, to be patient, believe in our work and be good enough to win that Olympic gold medal,” she said.“I understood very early that I cannot compare with the best athletes. I was very honest and said ‘this will not work’ although I was very persistent. My abilities were not at the desired level. Then I said, ‘Okay, I like this sport. My sister was very talented back then. I think I will try to be a coach’," Jelena said about her journey.While the younger sister is preparing herself for the Los Angeles Olympics, the elder sister is training her competitors in India. “We laugh about it. She would have wanted me with her, but she understands my professional commitments and is very proud of what I have been doing.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Neeraj Chopra’s replacement: Yashvir Singh drafted into India’s Asian Games javelin squad
articles.summary: More sports News: New Delhi: Glasgow Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has been drafted into India’s Asian Games athletics squad, replac.
articles.body: New Delhi: Glasgow Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has been drafted into India’s Asian Games athletics squad, replacing two-time Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, who was ruled out for the season following an ankle ligament tear.Yashvir, who recently threw a personal best of 85.41m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, will team up with the in-form Rohit Yadav (personal best 87.05m) to anchor India’s two-member men’s javelin campaign at Aichi-Nagoya.Meanwhile, former long jumper and Athletics Federation of India (AFI) senior vice-president Anju Bobby George will not travel as team leader, it’s been learnt. Though proposed by the AFI, her name was not cleared by the sports ministry adhering to its guidelines which say: IOA will ensure that any person, if he/she is holding elected position in EC of IOA, any NSF or any sports body, whose name has been included in the list of team officials, will be treated at no cost to the govt.The final athletics squad strength has been pruned to 77. Distance runner Abhishek Pal was dropped after testing positive for clomiphene. “It is not a case of returning dope positive, but as National Anti Doping Agency (NADA) investigates, we don’t want to take any risks,” said AFI planning committee chairman Lalit Bhanot. Additionally, 110m hurdler Tejas Shirse was ruled out due to foot stress fractures suffered during CWG.These two exclusions offset the latest addition of six athletes — Harita Bhadra (200m), Kiran Pahal (400m), Sindhushree G (pole vault), I Asha Ilango (triple jump), Sanya Yadav (discus), and Praveen Kumar (hammer throw) — who were cleared by the ministry after the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) accepted IOA’s late request for their addition, bringing the count from 73 to 79 before Pal and Shirse’s omissions brought the contingent size down to 77.AFI is also seeking approval for Hangzhou double-medallist Avinash Sable to compete in the 5,000m alongside his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event. However, Sable must first breach the AFI qualification mark of 13:39.18s at the Indian Athletics Series Finals here on Sept 10, where most Asian Games-bound athletes will compete.Know Yashvir-- Born in Devsar, Haryana and raised in Jaipur, Raj.-- Shifted from basketball to javelin at age 13, initially practicing with bamboo javelins.-- Coached by his father Rai Singh, a former Indian Railways national champion.-- Broke Chopra’s U-20 Federation Cup record in 2021; joined the 80m club in 2022 (82.13m).-- Overcame major shoulder surgery in late 2023 that kept him out for nearly a year.-- Claimed bronze at Glasgow CWG with a final-throw personal best of 85.41m.-- Became only the third Indian male javelin medallist in CWG history after Kashinath Naik and Chopra.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jonny Brownlee retires from triathlon at 36
articles.summary: Jonny Brownlee, a former Olympic triathlon champion and six-time world champion, says "it's over for professional sport".
articles.body:
Former world and Olympic champion Jonny Brownlee has retired at the age of 36.

The Briton won Olympic bronze at London 2012, silver at Rio 2016 and gold in the mixed relay at Tokyo 2020.

He is also a six‑time world champion and won mixed team relay gold at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Brother Alistair, a double Olympic champion, retired at the age of 36 in 2024.

"I've been thinking about it for a while. I've won more than I ever thought I'd ever achieve," Jonny told BBC Sport.

"One thing I'm really proud of is we full on committed to winning Olympic medals and delivering our best performance. And now I just don't think I can do that any more.

"It's over for professional sport, but I don't think you ever truly stop."

Brownlee said the birth of his son Freddie 10 months ago clarified his plans for the future.

"I don't think I can have that commitment because of how life is. He's my priority now, my family, but also with my body as well," said Brownlee.

"The thought of missing a training session used to be the worst thing in the world, whereas now, if Freddie is ill or needs me, then without question I do that.

"I used to have absolutely no fear with racing. I used to dive into corners on my bike at 60kph and not care.

"If I hit that corner and crash, then I can't hold Freddie for five to six weeks if I have got a broken wrist. I was asking if that was really worth it any more."

In a glittering career, Brownlee said the moments that resonate most are London 2012 and the World Series coming to his home city of Leeds in 2016.

"To deliver those medals [in 2012] was something I'm incredibly proud of," he said.

"The first time racing in Leeds kind of symbolised everything, the whole journey.

"The fact that there was a World Series in Leeds was just unthinkable when we started triathlon, and then to come into the Millennium Square for the first time was one of the proudest moments of my life and something I'll never forget."

Brownlee said sharing such a long career alongside Alistair was "unbelievably special", but that the famous 2016 World Series Triathlon race in Mexico played on his mind.

Jonny was leading when his legs started to give way on the run leg in gruelling heat.

Alistair, who was in third at the time, propped Jonny up for the final 700m and helped him over the line.

"It really annoyed me at the start. I've got multiple Olympic medals, world championships - and that got remembered," said Brownlee.

"Quite often now people say 'Which one are you? Are you the one who did the carrying or the one who got carried?' So yeah, it does grate me a little bit."

However, Brownlee said he is "proud" of the moment and that it underlined the importance of helping others.

Brownlee said he knew there was one medal left to claim before he stepped away - an Olympic gold.

Brownlee said he "committed everything" and "used my last bits of energy" to take mixed triathlon gold alongside Jessica Learmonth, Georgia Taylor-Brown and Alex Yee at the Tokyo Olympics.

"If I hadn't won that Olympic gold medal I think there would always be something missing," he said.

He said winning gold was the moment he was "finally known as Jonny Brownlee, and not as the person who came 10, 15 seconds behind Alistair".

"I'm incredibly proud that we've had an impact on the sport," he said.

"It's time to move on because I wouldn't be doing myself justice by doing it half-heartedly any more.

"Although they are saying I'm retiring from professional racing, I'm definitely not stopping the sport. If anything, I'm actually going to race more."

However, Brownlee said he is "proud" of the moment and that it underlined the importance of helping others.

Brownlee said he knew there was one medal left to claim before he stepped away - an Olympic gold.

Brownlee said he "committed everything" and "used my last bits of energy" to take mixed triathlon gold alongside Jessica Learmonth, Georgia Taylor-Brown and Alex Yee at the Tokyo Olympics.

"If I hadn't won that Olympic gold medal I think there would always be something missing," he said.

He said winning gold was the moment he was "finally known as Jonny Brownlee, and not as the person who came 10, 15 seconds behind Alistair".

"I'm incredibly proud that we've had an impact on the sport," he said.

"It's time to move on because I wouldn't be doing myself justice by doing it half-heartedly any more.

"Although they are saying I'm retiring from professional racing, I'm definitely not stopping the sport. If anything, I'm actually going to race more."

articles.title: Caitlin Clark, Paige Bueckers lead Team USA to strong win over China in debuts at 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup
articles.summary: The veterans got Team USA a lead Friday and the youngsters closed it out with authority.
articles.body:
All the pressure is on Team USA at the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup. After winning the event four straight times, that's now the expectation for newcomers like Paige Bueckers and Caitlin Clark.

In their first test as a team, the U.S. proved it was more than capable, defeating China 94-61 on Friday. In the process, Clark and Bueckers showed they are more than ready to represent Team USA.

It was a mostly smooth ride for Team USA, which led by roughly 20 points for the majority of the contest. On the offensive side, Jackie Young and Rhyne Howard led the way for the Americans early before Clark and Bueckers finished late. Young, who started the contest, finished with 12 points and three assists in the victory. Howard, who came off the bench, helped the team build its lead early, finishing with 14 points.

For all of Team USA's excellence Friday, there was one moment in the contest where the U.S. hit resistance. In the second quarter, China went on an 11-3 run after switching to a zone defense. During a halftime interview, Team USA coach Kara Lawson admitted that China's defense "stymied" her team briefly.

But Team USA found its way through that wall, eventually taking a 20-point lead into halftime. It was able to push that lead in the second half.

With the game in hand, the reserves saw more time in the third and fourth quarters and did not disappoint. After a quiet first half, Bueckers came alive late, finishing with 14 points, her first of which came after a smooth steal.

Clark also made her presence felt, though not as a scorer initially. During the first half, Clark acted as a distributor, racking up assists and finding the open player. Once Team USA shifted to its youth lineup in the second half, Clark started firing up shots, eventually tying for the team lead in points.

Along the way, she managed to hit one of her patented, long-range 3s.

She also continued shelling out assists, eventually securing a double-double (14 points, 11 assists) in her first-ever FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup game.

Angel Reese did her usual thing, playing relentless defense and pulling down rebounds. She finished with five points and eight rebounds in the win.

By the end of the contest, every single member of Team USA scored. Sonia Citron — another member of the team's youth movement — was the last to secure a bucket, finishing with two points.

It was a play that perfectly encapsulated why Team USA is going to be a problem for its opposition at the event.

It was an encouraging debut from that group, and from the team generally. While that was always the expectation, the team did hit some adversity Monday, when it was announced A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum would not play in the event due to injury .

Additionally, China wasn't necessarily going to be an easy win, as the team met the U.S. in the championship during the 2022 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup.

Despite all that, Team USA took care of business Friday. In the process, they proved why they are the favorites to once again win it all. The veterans played as expected, while the youngsters proved they were more than ready for the limelight.

Team USA will look to carry that momentum into its next game in the event, which will come against Italy on Sunday.
